subject: research/inference-substitution
professional: a statistician working on sequential and anytime-valid testing who also reviews verifiable-inference / ML-security papers (the reviewer for a paper like Gao, Liang and Guestrin 2024, 'Model equality testing'); first checks: is the e-process valid under H0, what does the verifier have to know, do the closed forms and the simulations agree, and what is the nearest prior work on square-root detectability laws and on auditing model substitution

evidence.correctness: Re-ran `PYTHONPATH=src python3 experiments/run.py` (6.8 s) and diffed it against experiments/results.txt: identical. Independent recomputation in scratchpad is_check.py (40-digit Decimal arithmetic, own Zipf/tilt/KL/chi2, does not import the package): E1 KL and chi2 for beta 0.3/0.5/0.7/0.9 match to 4 decimals (0.3308/0.7440 ... 0.0075/0.0152); L = ln(16/0.05) = 5.768; E3 theory L/KL(mix_p||P) 126, 344, 764, 1349, 3012, 6117, 11947, 24316 and small-p law 118 ... 24157 all match; KL(mix)/(p^2 chi2/2) is 0.94 to 0.99, so the small-p approximation the paper uses holds. E5 savings ceilings 3938/5440/9062/27586 and audit rates 0.155/0.296/0.821/7.610 (B=10000) and 0.017/0.033/0.091/0.846 (B=30000) match. E6: I derived f* = (hK/(2Nc))^{2/3} by setting d/df [fNc + hK f^{-1/2}] = 0 and minimised the cost with my own golden-section search: all nine f* and costs match (e.g. h=5, c=0.1: 0.2645, 79337 vs 127200 at f=1). Wald's identity confirms savings_curve's p*s*E[min(T,N)] equals the expected number of cheated queries before the stopping time. Own Monte Carlo (is_mc.py: own e-process in log space, own sampler, seed 20261122): false alarms 3.25% at alpha=0.05 over 400 runs (paper 1.5%; both below alpha); mean delay 217 at p=0.3 and 1955 at p=0.1, ratios 0.63 and 0.65 to the L/KL formula, inside the reported 0.52-0.79. The ratio is explained: measured delay sits between ln(1/alpha)/KL (179, 1564) and ln(G/alpha)/KL, as a mixture over a grid should. One mis-attribution: the N=64000 truncation is caused by run.py's simulated p list (floor 0.035, run.py:27), not the test grid floor 0.02 as the paper says.

evidence.claims: Backed: every number in README and whitepaper sections 2-4 (recomputed above); 'false alarms stay below alpha'; '10 tests'; 'measured 0.5-0.8x the formula'; 'x7.75 for x64 queries' (382.9/49.4); 'formula ~1.6x high' (1.55-1.80); stated limits (small-p heuristic, i.i.d. tokens, fixed p, no stake model, 'Stylised'). Not backed or missing a limit: (a) the verifier's statistic r = Q(x)/P(x) (model.py:70) assumes the verifier knows the substitute Q exactly; section 1 and the limitations (whitepaper.md:9, :31) say only that the verifier must evaluate P. When the cheater serves a different cheap model than the test assumes (Q = P^1.5 against a test built for P^0.5) the best grid component has negative drift (-0.006 per query at p=1) and 0 of 20 runs were detected within 20000 queries, even at full substitution, while the README presents the test as detecting substitution. (b) The paper's contributions line (whitepaper.md:31) presents the 1/p^2 delay and sqrt(N) theft law as contributions with no prior work cited. (c) whitepaper.md:21 attributes the N=64000 truncation to the test grid instead of the simulated p list.
evidence.fitness: Job: a researcher designing verifier sampling for a decentralised inference network wants the audit rate needed against a substituting provider. They get reproducible code and closed forms for one known substitute. They cannot use the test as is: it is a likelihood-ratio test against a known Q, and in practice Q is unknown (any of many cheaper or quantised models), which is exactly the setting of the nearest prior work: Gao, Liang and Guestrin 2024 ('Model equality testing: which model is this API serving?', MMD two-sample tests on API outputs), Cai et al. 2025 ('Are you getting what you pay for? Auditing model substitution in LLM APIs'), TOPLOC (Ong et al. 2025, locality-sensitive hashing of activations for verifiable inference) and SVIP (Sun et al. 2024). The square-root law itself is the known square-root law of steganographic capacity (Ker 2007; Filler, Ker and Fridrich 2009) and of covert communication (Bash, Goeckel and Towsley 2013): a sender can hide O(sqrt N) changes in N uses because detectability needs n p^2 chi^2 of order 1. The audit-rate trade-off is classical inspection-game territory (Avenhaus, von Stengel and Zamir 2002). None is cited (references from memory, not re-checked here). The result is sound as an instance of that law, not new, and the transfer to model substitution is a short note rather than a paper.
evidence.domain: Against sequential-testing practice the core is right: each factor has mean 1 under H0, the grid mixture is a nonnegative martingale, Ville gives the alpha bound, and empirical false alarms are below alpha. Departures a reviewer would hit in the first hour: a simple (known-Q) alternative presented as a substitution detector, no composite or nonparametric alternative (a universal-inference or plug-in e-process with Q estimated from checked tokens would be the standard fix); the delay constant is a loose upper bracket (measured 0.5-0.8x) where the standard mixture analysis gives ln(1/alpha)/KL plus a grid/log term; single-token i.i.d. model with no real model outputs, although research/CLAUDE.md asks for theory checked on real data or industrial-grade open tools. It does not reach the PhD bar in research/CLAUDE.md.

defects.what: The detector is a likelihood-ratio test against a known substitute: r = Q(x)/P(x) requires the verifier to know Q exactly, but the paper says only that the verifier must evaluate P. When the provider serves a different cheap model (P^1.5 against a test built for P^0.5) the best grid component drifts downward and 0 of 20 full-substitution runs are detected in 20000 queries. Every audit rate in E5/E6 holds only for a known Q.

No prior work cited. The sqrt(N) theft law is the square-root law of steganographic capacity (Ker 2007; Filler, Ker and Fridrich 2009) and of covert communication (Bash, Goeckel and Towsley 2013); model-substitution auditing has Gao, Liang and Guestrin 2024 and Cai et al. 2025; verifiable inference has TOPLOC and SVIP; audit-rate trade-offs are inspection games (Avenhaus et al. 2002). The contributions line presents these as new.

The E4 and E6 headline computations are untested: savings_curve has no test (dropping the factor p or zeroing undetected runs both survive), and the only f_star test uses h=20, c=0.05, where f* hits the min(1.0, ...) cap, so removing the factor 2 from the formula survives.
The N=64000 truncation is attributed to 'the very edge of our test's grid' (floor 0.02), but p* = 0.0215 is above that floor; the row is truncated because run.py simulates no p below 0.035.

Single-token i.i.d. Zipf model only; no check on real model outputs (e.g. logprobs of an open model and its quantised version), which research/CLAUDE.md asks for, and the delay constant is only an upper bracket (measured 0.5-0.8x) without the standard ln(1/alpha)/KL lower bracket.

verdict: A small, clean, fully reproducible note: run.py reproduces results.txt byte for byte, every closed-form number in E1, E3, E5 and E6 recomputes with independent 40-digit arithmetic and an independent minimiser, and an independent Monte Carlo agrees on false alarms (below alpha) and on the delay ratio. It does not meet the bar. Verification is 2: 3 of 5 seeded mutants survive, including the lines that compute the sqrt-law savings and f*. Claims are 2: the detector needs the substitute Q to be known, which is unstated, and with a different cheap model it never fires (0/20 at full substitution). As research the sqrt(N) law is the known square-root law of steganography and covert communication, and the paper cites none of that work or the model-substitution auditing literature, so it is a sound instance of a known result, not a new one.
